passage:
Zeenat,
I'm writing this instead of texting because texting is kind of the problem.
Last Saturday you didn't reply for three hours and I checked my phone about fifty times. By the time you answered, I'd already decided you were bored of me. So I posted that photo with a friend from tuition just to see if you'd get jealous. That was a test, and it wasn't fair to you.
Here's what I'm trying now. When the dread starts, I put the phone in the drawer, go for a run round the colony, and tell myself: no reply is not a no. It works a little better each time.
I really like being close to you. I just don't want my panic to crowd us.
Pranav

qa.q: How long did Zeenat take to reply last Saturday?
qa.a: Zeenat didn't reply for three hours.

qa.q: What was Pranav afraid of during those three hours?
qa.a: Pranav feared that Zeenat had become bored and was pulling away, which is why the checking felt so urgent.

qa.q: What turning point does Pranav describe, and why might it help?
qa.a: Pranav now puts the phone in a drawer and goes for a run when the dread starts, which calms the panic before it turns into another test.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt seeing the photo that was posted as a test?
qa.a: Zeenat may have felt confused or hurt at being tested without knowing why, which is why Pranav calls it unfair.

grounding: A teenager admits to constant message-checking, dread at a slow reply and a jealousy test, and describes learning to calm down alone.

passage: Didi, you're the only one I can tell this to. So Manoj and I have been talking for two months. When he's online and doesn't reply, my chest goes tight, like something's wrong. Last week I sent him six messages in ten minutes. Six! Then I told him Sameer from class had asked me out, which isn't even true, just to see if he'd care. He went quiet for a whole day and I felt awful. Now I've made a rule. When I want to send a second message, I stop, make chai, and text you instead. And yesterday I told Manoj straight, "I get scared when you don't reply. Can you just say busy?" He said okay. Honestly, didi, the Indu from last week would never.

qa.q: How many messages did Indu send in ten minutes?
qa.a: Indu sent six messages in ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Indu's tight chest suggest when Manoj is online but silent?
qa.a: It suggests Indu feels dread that something is wrong between them, even without any real sign.

qa.q: What new rule helps Indu, and why?
qa.a: Before a second message, Indu stops, makes chai and texts didi instead, which calms the alarm long enough to think.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when he heard the made-up story about Sameer?
qa.a: He was likely hurt or confused, which may be why he went quiet for a whole day.

grounding: A teenager confides dread at unanswered messages and a jealousy test, then describes pausing to self-soothe and asking directly.

passage: Xin's thumb hovered over the screen on the tram home through Copenhagen. Three texts to Anders since lunch, and not one from him. The fourth was typed: "Are you ignoring me?" She deleted it, put the phone face down on her knee and breathed slowly until the tram reached her stop. At home she wrote a different message: "Honestly, when I don't hear back, I get scared you're losing interest. Could you just send a quick 'busy' when you are?" Then she went to choir practice, where she had a solo to learn, and forgot to check her phone for an hour. When she looked, Anders had replied: "Sorry, football ran late. Yes, I can do that. Sing well."

qa.q: What did Xin's fourth text say before she deleted it?
qa.a: It said, "Are you ignoring me?"

qa.q: What was Xin worried about when Anders didn't reply?
qa.a: She was scared that Anders was losing interest, and she named that fear in her new message.

qa.q: What was the turning point on the tram, and why did it help?
qa.a: She deleted the fourth text and breathed until her stop, which gave her time to calm down and ask clearly instead of accusing.

qa.q: How might Anders have felt reading the calm request instead of "Are you ignoring me?"
qa.a: He probably found it easy to say yes, since it asked for something simple rather than blaming him.

grounding: A teenager stops before a fourth text, names her fear, asks plainly for what she needs and turns to her own interest in singing.

passage:
In the school counsellor's room, Himani sat twisting her ID card strap. "Rekha's always with the new basketball girls now. I've messaged her three times since yesterday."
"And a fourth is waiting?" the counsellor asked.
Himani laughed shakily. "Typed already."
"What's the fear under it?"
Himani was quiet. "That I'll have nobody if she drifts."
"That's a real fear. What could you ask her for, directly?"
"Maybe... one lunch a week, just us."
She sent that instead of the fourth text. On the way out she stopped at the notice board and wrote her name on the sign-up sheet for the Saturday pottery club. Rekha's reply came before the bell: "Wednesday lunches? Yes!!"

qa.q: Which club did Himani sign up for?
qa.a: She signed up for the Saturday pottery club.

qa.q: What was Himani afraid of underneath the urge to send a fourth text?
qa.a: She feared she would have nobody if Rekha drifted away.

qa.q: Which choice changed the outcome, and why?
qa.a: Himani asked Rekha directly for one lunch a week instead of sending a fourth message, which gave Rekha something easy to say yes to.

qa.q: How might Rekha have seen a clear request for lunch compared with many worried messages?
qa.a: She likely found it easy and welcome, which shows in her eager reply.

grounding: With a counsellor's questions, a teenager pauses before a fourth message, names her fear, asks her friend directly and joins a club of her own.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage:
Friday: Bidisha's reply to Mehak's long message about the weekend was just "ok." Mehak stared at it in the college canteen until her tea went cold. By evening she had sent, "If you're done with me, just say it."
Saturday: Bidisha called, confused. She had been stuck in a lab all day. Mehak's face burned. "I don't know why I said that," she muttered, and spent most of the afternoon under her quilt, sick with shame.
Two weeks later: another short "ok" arrived. Mehak felt the same drop in her stomach, and this time she noticed it. She wrote, "Small panic here, not your fault. Are we still on for Sunday?" Bidisha sent back, "Of course. Lab again. Sunday, samosas, you and me."

qa.q: What did Bidisha's first reply say?
qa.a: It was just "ok."

qa.q: What did Mehak feel on Saturday after Bidisha's call, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed; her face burned and she spent most of the afternoon under her quilt.

qa.q: What changed the second time a short reply arrived?
qa.a: Mehak noticed the drop in her stomach, named it as a small panic, and asked a simple question instead of lashing out.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt receiving "If you're done with me, just say it" after a long day in the lab?
qa.a: She was confused and probably hurt, since she had done nothing except be busy.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage: Ojas, beta, sit. Your Anand chacha was not always this calm, you know. At twenty-one I was in love with your chachi, and I was a mess. If she spoke to another boy in class, I'd go silent for days. If she was ten minutes late to the bus stand, I'd think, that's it, she's leaving. Once I shouted at her in front of the college gate for laughing at someone else's joke. Afterwards I couldn't look at her, I felt so small. She didn't leave. She sat me down and said, "I'm not going anywhere, but you can't shout at me." Slowly I started telling her, "I'm scared," instead of getting angry. Forty years married now. Still scared sometimes. I just say so.

qa.q: Where did Anand once shout at the woman he loved?
qa.a: He shouted at her in front of the college gate.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after shouting, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt ashamed; he couldn't look at her and felt very small.

qa.q: What turning point helped Anand change?
qa.a: She told him she wasn't leaving but that he couldn't shout at her, and he began saying "I'm scared" instead of getting angry.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Ojas's chachi when Anand went silent for days?
qa.a: She was likely confused and hurt, punished for ordinary things like talking in class or running late.

grounding: An uncle recalls reading small cues as rejection at twenty-one, lashing out, feeling shame and slowly softening with a steady partner.

passage:
"You were online at eleven. Who were you talking to?" Trisha asked before Siddharth had even taken off his shoes.
"My brother. About Papa's knee."
"You could have messaged me."
Siddharth felt the old urge to hand her the phone, or to walk straight back out. He did neither.
"Trish, I love you. I'm not hiding anything. But I'm not going to show you my chats every night. It makes me feel watched."
"So you won't show me."
"No. But here's what I will do. I'll message you when I reach the office and before I leave. Every day. Can we try that?"
Silence. "And if I panic anyway?"
"Then tell me you're panicking, and I'll sit with you. I won't disappear."
Trisha let out a long breath. "Okay. Office and leaving."

qa.q: Who was Siddharth talking to at eleven?
qa.a: He was talking to his brother about Papa's knee.

qa.q: What did Siddharth feel when Trisha asked who he was talking to?
qa.a: He felt watched and uncomfortable, pulled either to prove himself by handing over the phone or to walk out.

qa.q: What choice did Siddharth make instead of giving in or pulling away?
qa.a: He stayed warm, set a clear limit about the chats, and offered steady messages twice a day, plus company when she panics.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel about the offer to sit with her if she panics?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that her fear is welcomed rather than punished, which is why she lets out a breath and agrees.

grounding: A man who feels watched by an anxious partner avoids both giving in and withdrawing, pairing warm consistency with a clear limit.

passage: I'm Rehana, and last winter I nearly ended things with Vaibhav without meaning to. He'd ask, "Do you still love me?" three times a day. If I went out with my friends, he'd call twice. I felt like I was always sitting an exam I could fail. So I started replying later and later, just to breathe. That made it worse. He got more frantic, sure I was leaving. One night I finally said, "I'm here. I love you. And I need Thursday evenings to myself, no calls." Then I kept both promises, every single week. It took a while. Now he texts "have fun" on Thursdays, and I come home wanting to tell him everything.

qa.q: How many times a day did Vaibhav ask "Do you still love me?"
qa.a: He asked it three times a day.

qa.q: What did Rehana feel when Vaibhav kept checking, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Rehana felt pressured and tested, like always sitting an exam that could be failed.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Replying later and later made Vaibhav more frantic; what helped was saying "I'm here, I love you" alongside a clear Thursday limit, and keeping both every week.

qa.q: How did Rehana's slower replies look from Vaibhav's side?
qa.a: To him they looked like proof that Rehana was leaving, so his fear grew and he became more frantic.

grounding: A partner describes feeling constantly tested, pulling away and deepening the fear, then finding that warm consistency with a clear limit works better.

"Bye, Uday. Amma's going to the market." Hansa waves at the door.
Uday doesn't look up from his stacking cups.
"He didn't even cry," Dadi says.
"He never does," Hansa says, and goes.
Later Uday bumps his head on the table. His lip trembles. He turns to the wall and pats the floor, alone.
Hansa comes home. "Oof, a bump? Come, raja."
Uday stays by the wall, very still.
"Maybe quiet doesn't mean fine," Dadi says softly.

He walked to the corner, turned his back and held his knee, breathing fast. When I came close, he shuffled away. I sat nearby and said, "That hurt. I'm right here." After a while he leaned on my arm. Plan: stay close in hard moments; tell his father at pickup.

passage: In a small flat in Marseille, five-year-old Clara wrestles with her boot buckle. "I do it!" she snaps when her mother, Rania, kneels to help. The buckle won't close. I'll wait here in case you want a hand." Clara tries twice more. Then, without looking up, she pushes one foot toward her mother.

passage: On sports day at the Shillong kindergarten, the other children ran to their parents after the sack race. Lalremsiami, five, walked to the water table alone and poured her own cup, spilling half. "I can do it," she told Mr Francis before he could help. Her mother hadn't been able to come. When she tripped on the way back, she jumped up fast, eyes wet, and wiped them hard. Mr Francis crouched and opened his arms. She shook her head and stepped away. "Okay," he said. "Want to hold the finish-line ribbon with me instead?" She nodded and took one end.

passage: At the community centre's after-school room, the boys picking football teams called every name but Chaitanya's. "Don't care," he said, and dropped onto the beanbag with the old tablet, thumbs flying through a racing game. Vandana, who ran the centre, watched his jaw tighten each time the ball thumped outside. She didn't ask him to talk. She sat on the next beanbag and started sorting coloured pencils. "Being left out stinks sometimes," she said to nobody in particular. "If you ever feel like telling me about it, I'm here till six." Chaitanya kept racing. At quarter to six, without looking up, he said, "They always pick me last." Vandana nodded. "Thanks for telling me."

passage: My little sister Neelam, nine, found out today that the whole class got invited to Pooja's party except her. Mummy didn't push. She just said, "If it bothers you later, you can tell me. Or not. Either is fine." Later I heard Neelam in Mummy's room, talking in a small voice. I couldn't hear what she said. I'm Kalyani, by the way. I left my last chocolate on her pillow.

passage:
Tuesday night. Hansa again today. Her pencil box spilled across the floor in maths and she just picked everything up, face blank. No fuss, no "Ma'am, help." She never asks. When Karthik tore her chart by accident, she said "It's fine" and turned to the window. Is it fine? I honestly don't know.
So I tried something small. At lunch I sat at the next desk, not beside her, marking books. I asked, "Glue stick or tape for your chart?" She chose tape. Then I just stayed there, marking. She fixed the chart and slid it an inch closer to my side of the desk.
Tomorrow: same time, same desk. No pushing.
Ishita

qa.q: What might Hansa be feeling when she says "It's fine" and turns to the window?

qa.a: Ishita sat at the next desk and offered a simple choice, giving steady company without pressure.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Hansa says "It's fine" after he tears her chart?
qa.a: Karthik might feel relieved, but also unsure whether Hansa is really okay, since she turns away.

grounding: A teacher's diary notes a child who never asks for help and seems fine during upsets, and tries a quiet check-in with a choice and steady presence.

passage: In the one-storey school at the edge of the sugarcane fields, Kamal sir had been watching Noor for weeks. When rain leaked through the roof onto her notebook, she dried it on her sleeve and said nothing. When other children crowded round him with questions, she sat back, sums done or not. He didn't call her out. Every morning he stopped by her bench: "Slate or notebook today?" Every afternoon he sat on the verandah step till the bus came, reading. After a month, Noor sat down two steps away. The next week, one step. One afternoon she held out her notebook. "Sir, this sum. I don't get it."

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to finally say "Sir, this sum"?

passage: After basketball in Vancouver, Tuan sat on the bench, spinning his ball, and said, "Can I tell you something? My parents are splitting up. And... you're kind of my best friend." Alejandro's stomach tightened. He laced his shoes very slowly. "Cool. I mean, that's rough." For three days he answered Tuan's texts with one word and took the long way home. Keeping things light felt safer, somehow. On Friday he saw Tuan eating lunch alone. He sat down, stared at his sandwich and said, "Sorry I went weird. I'm bad at serious stuff. But... you're my best friend too." Tuan grinned. "Took you three days." "Small steps," Alejandro muttered.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt during the three days of one-word texts?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and alone, having just shared something painful and getting little back.

grounding: A teenager pulls back when a friendship turns emotional, then takes a small step toward openness by admitting the friendship matters.

passage: Study hour at the Panaji boarding school. Maria slid a note across the desk: "You've been quiet since your Nana's surgery. Want to talk after?" Lokesh folded it into a tiny square. Talking meant her worried eyes on him, and him owing her something back. He wrote, "I'm handling it." When the bell rang he left by the back stairs. That night in the dorm he lay awake, the note still in his pocket. The next evening, before he could change his mind, he wrote one line on a fresh page and passed it over: "Nana's okay now. I was scared." Maria wrote under it, "Thanks for telling me. That's enough." Something in his chest loosened.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Lokesh left by the back stairs?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out and worried, since she had reached out kindly.

grounding: A teenager at boarding school pulls back from a caring friend and handles a worry alone, then practises being open in one small line.
